lines.text: Scientists once watched a group of hunter-gatherers sleep for twenty nights.
In all that time, everyone was asleep at the same moment for just eighteen minutes.
Eighteen minutes. In twenty nights.
So how did ancient humans actually sleep?
Where did they lie down? Who kept the lions away? And did they really sleep like we do?
The answer is weirder than you think.
Meet Moss. He's a Stone Age human, and he is very, very tired.
Tonight, we're going to follow him to bed.
Let's start with our cousins.
Every evening, a wild chimpanzee climbs a tree and builds itself a fresh bed of bent branches and leaves.
It takes just a few minutes.
At some point, our ancestors came down from the trees for good.
And sleeping on the ground comes with a problem.
Things with teeth.
Lions, leopards, hyenas. The night belonged to them.
So humans did something no other animal does.
They brought fire to bed.
In Wonderwerk Cave, in South Africa, scientists found ash and burned bone about a million years old.
That's one of the earliest signs of fire being used inside a cave.
Fire meant warmth. It meant light. And it may have helped keep hungry animals at a distance.
Scientists think it also gave people something new: evenings.
Time to sit together, share food, and tell stories, after the sun went down.
But a fire doesn't make a bed.
And this is where the evidence gets surprisingly cosy.
In Border Cave, in South Africa, archaeologists found the remains of beds made around two hundred thousand years ago.
They are the oldest known grass beds ever found.
They were made of bundles of broad-leafed grass, laid near the back of the cave, close to the fire.
The warmest, safest spot in the house.
But here's the clever part.
Underneath the grass, there was a layer of ash.
Scientists think the ash was a bug barrier.
Crawling insects struggle to move through fine powder, and ash can clog up the tiny holes they breathe through.
On one bed, they even found burned bits of camphor bush, a plant that people in South Africa still use to keep insects away.
And when a bed got old and buggy?
They seem to have burned it. Then they laid fresh grass on top of the ashes.
Stone Age spring cleaning.
Fast forward to about seventy-seven thousand years ago, at another South African site called Sibudu.
Here, people stacked up mattresses of sedges and rushes, picked from a nearby river.
Some covered up to three square metres. Big enough to sleep on, sit on, and work on during the day.
And on top, they added leaves from a tree called the river wild-quince.
Those leaves contain natural chemicals that kill insects, and they'd be good at repelling mosquitoes.
So these people had soft beds, bug spray, and a fire.
But they still had one big problem. Who stays awake to watch for danger?
To find out, let's go back to those eighteen minutes.
The study was done with the Hadza, hunter-gatherers who live in Tanzania today.
They sleep in groups of twenty to thirty, outside by the hearth or in huts of grass and branches.
Thirty-three adults wore little watch-like sensors on their wrists for twenty days.
Here's the funny part. Nobody was given the job of night guard.
The Hadza generally don't post lookouts at all.
Instead, people's body clocks were naturally different.
Some were night owls. Some were early birds. And some just woke up a lot.
Older adults, in their fifties and sixties, tended to go to bed earlier and wake up earlier.
So at almost any moment of the night, someone was awake, or only lightly asleep.
Scientists call this the sentinel idea.
Your grumpy, early-rising grandpa might have been the best security system the Stone Age had.
Of course, the Hadza aren't time travellers. They're modern people with their own lives.
But studying them gives scientists clues about how humans slept before electric lights.
And those clues bust a few of our favourite myths.
In another study, scientists tracked the sleep of three groups: the Hadza, the San in the Kalahari, and the Tsimane in Bolivia.
You might expect them to sleep ten hours a night.
Nope. They slept between about five point seven and seven point one hours.
That's about the same as many people in modern cities, or even a bit less.
And they didn't go to bed when it got dark.
On average, they fell asleep more than three hours after sunset.
So what told them it was bedtime?
Scientists think the big clue was temperature.
They slept as the night cooled, and they usually woke up around the coldest part, just before sunrise.
And here's the one that might make you jealous.
The San and the Tsimane don't even have a word for insomnia.
Only a few people in every hundred said they regularly had trouble sleeping.
Wait. Didn't people in the past sleep in two halves?
You might have heard about first sleep and second sleep.
Historian Roger Ekirch found hundreds of mentions of it in old European diaries, letters and court records.
People went to bed, woke up for an hour or so in the middle of the night, then went back to sleep.
But that's from the last few hundred years, mostly in Europe, where winter nights are long.
The hunter-gatherers in these studies mostly slept in one stretch.
So for the Stone Age, the jury is still out.
And then there's the strangest idea of all.
In 2020, two scientists suggested that early humans in a Spanish cave, about four hundred thousand years ago, might have survived harsh winters by hibernating.
Like bears.
They pointed to odd marks on the bones that look a bit like those in hibernating animals.
But many experts aren't convinced. Those marks could have other causes, and big animals like us are bad at true hibernation.
So file that one under fun, but probably not.
So, here's what a night might have looked like for Moss.
A fire crackling at the back of the cave.
A soft bed of grass on a layer of ash, with bug-repelling leaves on top.
Friends and family lying close together, chatting long after sunset.
Sleep as the air turns cool. Up before the sun.
And somewhere in the group, there's always someone half awake. Listening.
Remember those eighteen minutes?
If the Hadza are any guide, our ancestors' camps were almost never all asleep at once.
We took turns without even trying.
So the next time a tiny noise wakes you at three in the morning, don't be annoyed.
You're just working your ancient night shift.
Follow for more of how ancient humans really lived.
